title: Identity and Individuality in Quantum Theory

summaries.example: Imagine two brand-new toy blocks made in the same factory. They look exactly alike, but you can still point to one on the left and one on the right. In ordinary life, we treat them as two individuals. Quantum physics asks whether tiny particles always work this way. For some quantum descriptions, swapping two matching particles does not make a new situation.
summaries.summary: The entry asks what quantum physics tells us about the identity of tiny objects. In daily life, we think of objects as separate individuals. Classical physics can describe matching particles as individuals because swapping them can count as a different arrangement. Quantum physics treats swaps differently: for particles of the same kind, the swap does not produce a new measurable arrangement. This has led to the idea that quantum particles may be non-individuals. Other accounts say the particles remain individuals, perhaps because of their relations, histories, locations, or features not captured by ordinary properties. Still other views focus on structures and patterns rather than objects. The central lesson is that the physical theory may fit more than one metaphysical picture, so physics alone may not settle what individuality ultimately is.
key_ideas: Everyday objects such as trees, rocks, and people are usually treated as individuals.
Quantum particles of the same kind can have the same basic properties, such as mass and charge.
Quantum statistics do not count every swap of matching particles as a new arrangement.
Some philosophers think this supports non-individuality; others think the particles can still be individuals.
The physics may not decide which philosophical picture is correct.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic shows that science and philosophy can work together. A theory may predict what measurements will happen without answering every question about what kinds of things exist. Studying quantum particles also teaches us to be careful with familiar words such as “object,” “same,” and “different.”

important_terms.definition: A single thing that can be counted as one and can be told apart, or treated as having its own identity.
Being impossible to tell apart using the properties or measurements being considered.
The idea that if two things have every relevant property in common, they must really be the same thing.
A change in the mathematical description that swaps matching particles but does not change the possible measurement results.
A view that matching quantum particles may not have separate identities in the ordinary sense.

questions_to_think_about: Can two things be different even when they have exactly the same properties?
Does being in a different place give a thing its own identity?
If a swap makes no difference to any measurement, should we say that anything really changed?
Can science leave more than one idea about what the world is like?

summaries.example: Consider two same-type fermions prepared in a joint state. A classical description might label them and count the arrangement with particle A in one state and particle B in another as different from the arrangement after swapping the labels. Quantum permutation invariance says that the swap does not create a distinct measurable state. One interpretation takes this to show that the particles lack individual identities. Another says the particles are individuals, with their distinctness grounded in relations or in a different account of which states are physically available.
summaries.summary: The entry examines whether quantum entities should be understood as individuals. For ordinary objects, individuality may be grounded in different properties, locations, substances, primitive thisness, or self-identity. Quantum particles of the same type share intrinsic features, and the Indistinguishability Postulate says that exchanging them does not alter measurement probabilities. The orthodox interpretation takes this to undermine the idea that the particles have identities that can be tracked across counterfactual arrangements. Several alternatives are discussed. Individuality might be primitive, grounded in weakly discerning relations, supported by a different interpretation of quantum mechanics, or associated with trajectories. A heterodox approach argues that same-type particles can sometimes be discerned through symmetric combinations of properties, while also raising problems about ambiguity and reidentification. Formal approaches such as quasi-set theory try to describe collections that can be counted without being ordered as ordinary individuals. Structuralist approaches shift attention from objects to relations and symmetries. Since these options can be compatible with the same physics, the entry describes a substantial underdetermination of metaphysics by quantum theory.
key_ideas: The debate begins with a distinction between numerical difference, measurable discernibility, and deeper conditions for identity.
Classical particle counting can support an individual-particle picture, but alternative representations weaken that conclusion.
The orthodox argument treats quantum permutation invariance as evidence for non-individuality.
Weak discernibility attempts to preserve individuality through relations, although critics question whether this truly explains distinctness.
A heterodox approach uses permutation-invariant properties to distinguish particles without assigning labels to particular particles.
Because several packages fit the physics, the entry presents quantum theory as metaphysically underdetermining.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate tests how far physical theories determine an ontology. It also clarifies the difference between a theory’s mathematical representation, its observable predictions, and claims about what fundamentally exists. The issue matters for realism: accepting quantum mechanics does not automatically select one account of whether electrons and other quanta are individuals.

important_terms.definition: The metaphysical status of an entity as a separate, countable object with conditions for being the same object.
A quantum principle stating that permuting same-type particles cannot produce a difference in measurement probabilities.
Invariance under exchanging the particle labels in a quantum description; the exchange does not represent a new observable state.

important_terms.term: Principle of the Identity of Indiscernibles
important_terms.definition: The thesis that no two individuals can share all the relevant properties and relations.
A non-qualitative basis of individuality, sometimes described as an irreducible “thisness.”
A relation-based form of distinguishability in which objects differ through an irreflexive relation, even without different individual properties.
The situation in which the physics is compatible with more than one broad metaphysical interpretation.
The view that the fundamental reality is organized by relations, patterns, and symmetries rather than by independently identified objects.

questions_to_think_about: Is numerical difference enough for individuality, or must an object also be reidentifiable across time and possible situations?
If a relation distinguishes two particles, does that relation explain their distinctness or already presuppose it?
Should properties of a whole quantum system be treated as reducible to properties of its parts?
When two interpretations make the same predictions, what non-empirical reasons could justify preferring one?
Does a theory describe objects, or can it describe only structures and symmetries?

summaries.example: Picture two identical-looking game pieces placed in two boxes. In a classical game, you might secretly mark them A and B, so switching their positions creates a new arrangement. In quantum physics, matching particles are not counted this way: the swapped description gives the same measurement possibilities. One philosopher may say the pieces were never separate individuals in the deep sense. Another may say they are individuals but that the theory restricts which arrangements are possible.
summaries.summary: This entry explores a difficult question: are electrons, photons, and other quantum entities individuals like coins or people? For everyday objects, we usually think identity comes from properties, location, substance, or a special “thisness.” But particles of the same type can share their intrinsic properties. In classical physics, secretly labeling particles means that switching them can produce a different arrangement. Quantum theory does not count such permutations as new measurable arrangements. The received view says this shows that quantum particles are non-individuals. Other philosophers argue that the same formalism can be interpreted differently. The particles might remain individuals because of relations, histories, trajectories, or the set of states allowed by the theory. A newer heterodox approach says particles can sometimes be distinguished using symmetric descriptions, although it faces questions about ambiguity and identity across time. Formal systems such as quasi-set theory try to represent collections that have a number but not an ordinary order. The entry concludes that physics may underdetermine the metaphysics: more than one account of individuality may fit the physical results.
key_ideas: Philosophers distinguish between being different things and being distinguishable by observable properties.
In classical physics, labels and positions can make swapped particles count as different arrangements.
Quantum statistics treat a swap of same-type particles as producing no new measurable arrangement.
This supports a received view of quantum non-individuality, but it is not the only interpretation.
Relations, histories, trajectories, or alternative quantum interpretations may support versions of individuality.
The same quantum theory can be connected with different metaphysical pictures.
summaries.why_it_matters: Quantum theory challenges assumptions that seem obvious in everyday life, especially the idea that every object must have a unique label. The debate also shows why interpreting science requires philosophical choices about identity, properties, relations, and mathematical representation. Understanding those choices helps us avoid treating one interpretation as if it were simply forced by the equations.

important_terms.definition: A thing regarded as one separate object, with its own identity.
Not able to be told apart by the properties or tests relevant to a discussion.
The claim that two things sharing all relevant features must be identical.
A mathematical exchange of particles in a description of a quantum system.
The idea that quantum particles may not be separate individuals in the usual everyday sense.
A way of distinguishing things by how they are related to one another rather than by separate properties.
When one set of physical facts fits more than one philosophical account of what exists.

questions_to_think_about: If two particles cannot be labeled in a physically meaningful way, are they still two individuals?
Can a relationship, such as having opposite spin directions, make two particles distinct?
Why might someone prefer a theory with fewer unneeded mathematical structures?
Could a scientific theory tell us how things behave without telling us exactly what things are?
What is gained or lost by describing quantum reality in terms of structures instead of objects?
